children: By Julie Zhu

Air cargo demand driven by AI data-centre projects shows no sign of slowing, according to the CEO of the world's largest air cargo handler, even as stock markets wobble over the sustainability of AI spending.
Kerry Mok, who runs Singapore-based SATS
, said capital equipment such as server racks and semiconductors has been the main driver of air cargo growth over the past year.
Some data-centre builds are multi-year projects, "which means there is a constant demand for that... It's good for us," he said in an interview on Wednesday.
The air cargo market is in the middle of its annual peak season and SATS is not experiencing any reduction in AI-related demand, Mok said. "The numbers are pretty robust."
The firm's cargo clients include Singapore Airlines
, Turkish Airlines and Atlas Air, according to its latest financial results presentation.

Mok said the Americas region was now SATS' fastest-growing market after a difficult prior year when tariffs and the removal of the "de minimis" exemption to duties on low-value packages weighed on US flows. "This year, our Americas are growing double digit, and it's coming back very nicely," he said.
He added that SATS was handling "a lot of data-centre products being shipped into the US" and has seen a surge in charter flights in and out of the country.

SATS, which also has catering and ground handling businesses, reported a 9% rise in revenue to S$1.71 billion ($1.33 billion) for the quarter ended September 30, on the back of higher cargo and meal volumes.
Its cargo volume growth outpaced International Air Transport Association benchmarks for the 12th straight quarter, rising 8% in the July-September period versus 5.3% global growth in IATA data.

Mok said the Middle East conflict led to a surge in cargo handling in Singapore, where volumes grew more than 8% in its first half ended September 30. That growth rate was "unheard of" for a city-state whose cargo growth normally tracks GDP, he said.
Charter flights have become "far more important" as Middle East carriers cancelled passenger flights, cutting belly-hold space for cargo, he added.

Mok said roughly 20% of the cargo SATS handles globally, mostly capital equipment, requires specialised treatment such as no vibration, tilting or double stacking. In Singapore, the share of technology cargo is even higher, he said.

The US said last week it would restrict shipments of advanced chips to Southeast Asian countries such as Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, which Chinese companies have used to access computing power to train AI models.
Mok played down the risk to air cargo volumes, saying demand exceeds supply.
"If it's a shortage of chip in one country, if suddenly I'm stopping the flow to that country, there'll be new demand elsewhere," he said.
($1 = 1.2896 Singapore dollars)
